name: Hair cloning

card.summary: Multiplying follicle cells in a lab to grow unlimited hair is a long-promised idea that remains in animal and lab research.
card.note: No approved product; commercial programmes have closed.

quick.overview:
Hair cloning would take cells from healthy follicles, multiply them in culture, and implant them to make new hair follicles, avoiding the donor limits of transplantation.

Per Wikipedia, it is in early stages, with milestones in mice and several company programmes ended.
quick.mechanism: Follicle-inducing cells such as dermal papilla cells, or iPSC-derived cells, are expanded in the lab and implanted to interact with scalp epithelium and form follicles.
quick.risks: No approved treatment exists, so no human safety record is cited. Obstacles listed include inconsistent hair direction, thin follicles and cycling shown only in mice.

lead: Hair cloning, also called hair multiplication or follicle neogenesis, is a proposed regenerative approach to hair loss. A small number of cells from healthy follicles, such as dermal papilla cells, are multiplied in the laboratory and implanted into balding scalp, where they are meant to form new follicles.[1][2] The aim is a fuller head of hair, including a restored hairline and crown, without being limited by how much donor hair a person has.

That limit is the central constraint of hair transplantation, which relocates existing follicles from the back and sides of the scalp. A cloning approach would in principle turn a small sample into a large number of follicles, and people who follow hair-loss forums often describe it as the technology that would change their options.[1][2] Wikipedia describes a University of Pennsylvania finding from 2012 that bald and non-bald scalp contain similar numbers of stem cells but that progenitor cells are depleted in bald areas, which is part of the rationale for cell-based approaches.[2]

As of the sources consulted, hair cloning remains in preclinical research, with milestones in mice and no approved product. Companies including Intercytex and Aderans ended their programmes, Stemson Therapeutics closed in December 2024, and a February 2026 RIKEN and OrganTech report described engineered follicles that cycled for 68 days in mice.[2]

chain: Take cells from a small scalp sample
Multiply follicle-inducing cells in the lab
Implant them into thinning or bald scalp
New follicles and fuller hair without donor-supply limits
angle.text: The intended payoff is hair density where a person has little: new follicles grown from a few cultured cells, for hairlines and crowns that transplantation cannot fully cover. So far, parts of the process have been shown in mice and in the laboratory.

paras: Proposed methods take dermal papilla cells or follicle stem cells from a small scalp sample, expand them in culture, and implant them where they are meant to induce new follicles through interaction with surrounding epithelial cells.[1] Newer lines of work use induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) made from patient cells, 3D cell aggregates and scaffolds, including 3D-printed biodegradable shafts.[1][2][3]

A related line of research studies wound-induced hair follicle neogenesis, a phenomenon in which full-thickness wounds in adult mammals regenerate new follicles. Reviews describe the signalling pathways involved and the process as similar to embryonic development.[4][5]

According to Wikipedia, Intercytex worked on cloning follicles from cells taken from the back of the neck and concluded in 2008 that it had not fully developed its therapy; the first artificial follicles grown from stem cells (2010) were thinner than normal; and Aderans Research Institute, whose Japanese trials continued into 2012, ended its funding in July 2013.[2] In 2012 University of Pennsylvania researchers reported that bald and non-bald scalp had similar stem cell numbers but depleted progenitor cells in bald areas.[2]

Reported later milestones include human-derived follicles grown in mice with inconsistent hair direction (2015), hair from iPSC-derived human skin implanted in mice (2016), permanent, naturally regenerating follicles grown in mice by Stemson Therapeutics and UC San Diego (July 2019), fully grown follicles cloned in mice at Yokohama National University (October 2022), and in February 2026 a RIKEN and OrganTech report identifying a third cell type, dermal condensate cells, with engineered follicles that produced 3 mm shafts and cycled for 68 days in mice.[2] A 2016 laboratory study generated iPSCs from human hair follicle keratinocytes as a potential source for follicle cloning.[3]

No studies found in humans demonstrating hair cloning as a treatment. Related work is laboratory and animal research, such as the iPSC study of follicle keratinocytes,[3] the mouse experiments described by Wikipedia,[2] and studies of wound-induced follicle neogenesis in mice.[4][5][6] A 2014 review of emerging alopecia treatments discusses cell-based and other approaches under study.[7]

Wikipedia lists inconsistent hair direction, thin follicles in earlier methods, depleted progenitor cells in bald scalp, and cycling shown only in mice as open problems.[2] Grokipedia, an AI-generated source, adds that results with related stem-cell injections are described as modest and inconsistent.[1]

timeline.event: Intercytex concludes its follicle therapy is not fully developed.[2]
First artificial follicles grown from stem cells, thinner than normal.[2]
University of Pennsylvania report on progenitor cell depletion in bald scalp.[2]
Aderans stops funding its hair multiplication research.[2]
iPSC-derived human skin produces hair in mice; iPSC study from follicle keratinocytes published.[2][3]
Stemson Therapeutics and UC San Diego grow follicles in mice with iPSC-derived cells.[2]
Yokohama National University reports fully grown follicles cloned in mice.[2]
RIKEN and OrganTech report dermal condensate cells and follicles cycling for 68 days in mice.[2]
